items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' — 'Hi Katie, how can I help you?' is a service opener, not a warm-up. The only human-temperature miss in an otherwise well-run open.

Storage stops and additional stops never asked. Both are low-probability on a one-bedroom local move, but the customer did volunteer that she is hauling her own artwork and antiques separately ('I will be moving those personally. I'll do it myself before you guys get here'), which is precisely the kind of statement that sometimes turns into a second address.

Moving stressors never asked. The customer spent the first three minutes of the call actively worried that Einstein cannot reach her — 'I think this will be an issue because if you guys need to reach me phone or like I don't know anything how is' — and Danah solved the logistics beautifully but never named the feeling or asked what else was on her mind about the move.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener. 'I'll quickly just quick do a quick rundown of the pricing then your estimate' sets up the block well but does not deliver the line.

The rate was framed per-team, not per-mover-per-hour: '$204 for two movers.' The rubric wants the per-mover math exposed so the customer understands what a third mover would cost and why the rate scales the way it does.

No Worries Damage Coverage was never named. She said 'insurance' inside the included list — 'the gas and the truck taxes and insurance' — and stopped there. The customer never heard $2,000, never heard 'repair, replace, or reimburse,' and never heard the 60¢/lb industry baseline that makes the coverage mean something. This is a free differentiator that costs one sentence and she was three words away from it.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned. The customer asked directly about arrival — 'on the day that they'll be here, will they give me a call?' and later 'The start time is when they're gonna start, not the appointment time, right?' — which is two separate invitations to say 'and if we miss the window we start discounting immediately.' Both went by.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email. She told the customer to check it, which is most of the value, but never said the key details are called out at the top — so the customer does not know to look there.
Truck count never stated. Mover count was given clearly; the truck was left implicit.

Additional stops and equivalents never covered as estimate variables. No school-bus-style anchor was used to make 2.5-3.5 hours feel concrete, though in fairness the estimate was already tight enough that it did not need much help.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10, and it is the biggest single gap in an otherwise strong call. The customer told her, unprompted, exactly two things that set it up: 'I haven't packed yet so I was planning to like pack and then give you guys a call' and 'those win, I do but I will be moving those personally. I'll do it myself before you guys get here.' She is already carloading. Nobody told her it saves money, nobody told her to do more of it, and nobody gave her the consolidation list — loose drawer items, closet odds and ends, pictures off the walls — that turns a 3.5-hour move into a 2.5-hour one.
No deposit and the booking ask are both absent, though both are genuinely inapplicable here — the customer booked online before the call and the move is already on the schedule for October 1st.
No business hours and no phone number given. 'Just give us a call' was the entire reach-us instruction.
Customer's name used twice — 'Hi Katie' and 'now that I have you on the phone, Katie' — short of the 3+ standard, on a call that ran eleven and a half minutes and had a dozen natural places for it.

No genuine rapport or humor moment. The warmth is real but it is all in the same register: 'Okay, perfect' appears eleven times. The customer made a small joke about her own sparse furniture — 'I don't even have a coffee table so it's not gonna be happy' — and it drew 'Okay, and what about valuable or fragile items.'
top_strength: This is the most rubric-disciplined call on the board, and the probe section is why. Danah is the only rep this week who asked for walk distance — and she asked for it at both ends, in two separate questions, with the follow-up: 'what is the walking distance from where we can park the truck up to the elevator on the first floor' and then 'what about the distance from the top from the second floor elevator to your unit?' She also asked the parking question at the destination ('Is there a driveway here that the trucking park or is it street parking?'), which is the variable that quietly adds thirty minutes to a job and which nobody else on this board touched. The specialty-items sweep was equally complete and asked in three separate passes rather than one catch-all: oversized and heavy ('anything that might be oversized or heavy like a safe or any exercise equipment?'), then valuable and fragile ('any artwork, any antique pieces or collection?'), then appliances ('are we gonna move major appliances fridge? Washer/Dryer'). The box question was the best on the board because it anchored first and asked second: 'typically for one bedroom apartment, there's about fifteen to 25 boxes there. So are we gonna boxes for you if so would you think you're gonna fall within that range?' That gives the customer a frame to answer inside, which is why she produced a real number (15-20) instead of a shrug — and Danah then protected the estimate on both ends: 'I'm gonna put you within that range but just in case it's gonna, if it's gonna be like crazy amount of boxes you can just let us know so we can update your profile and your estimate.' Her pricing block is the only complete one this week: '$204 for two movers. Everything's already included there, the gas and the truck taxes and insurance... So there are no hidden fees. There are no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no sterle or elevator fees and notice assembly and reassembly fees, so it's only the hourly rate.' Clock is a clean 4/4 — minimum, proration, and both ends of the billable window: 'the time we start once we get to your apartment and pick up the first item then the time will stop after we unload just reassemble everything into your new place.' She hit Meet Your Mover by name and unprompted. And underneath all of it, she opened the call by solving a real operational problem — a bad phone number that would have blown up the move-day call — and turned it into a backup contact with a note on the profile: 'I'm gonna put in a note here to try Alicia's phone number as well just in case we don't reach you.'
coaching_note: This is the call to hold up as the structural model for the team, and the coaching is almost entirely about three sentences she did not say. First and most valuable: the Save Your Ass speech is a complete zero on a customer who was already doing it. She said she is moving her own artwork and antiques and that she has not packed yet. That is a rep's ideal setup and it produced nothing. The line was: 'One thing that will save you real money — anything small and awkward you can take over yourself before we get there comes straight off the clock. The loose stuff in drawers, closet odds and ends, pictures off the walls. You are already doing that with your artwork, and every carload like that is fifteen or twenty minutes off your bill. Does that make sense?' On a $510-$714 job that is a meaningful percentage, and it is the section where her score is furthest from where the rest of the call sits. Second: On-Time Guarantee, which the customer opened the door for twice. 'The start time is when they're gonna start, not the appointment time, right?' is a customer telling you she is thinking about arrival timing. The answer should have ended with 'and if we ever miss the arrival window we start discounting immediately — that is our On-Time Guarantee.' Third: she said 'insurance' where she should have said 'No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace, or reimburse accidental damage, where most movers give you sixty cents a pound.' Same breath, same list, three times the value. Estimate accuracy: this one is a positive and should be recorded as such for the bottom-4 comparison work. She gave the typical range for the home size, placed the customer inside it rather than above it, and said why — 'based on the details you shared, I would estimate your move to fall within that typical range.' No padding, no 'to be safe,' no hedge above her own stated band. The math checks out against the rate she quoted (the transcript's '$51,014 to $714' is a transcription mangle of $510 to $714, which is exactly 2.5 and 3.5 hours at $204). This is the behavior the estimate-accuracy rock is trying to produce and it is worth pulling the actual against when this move completes on October 1st. Two small polish items: use the customer's name more than twice — she asked for it in the first sentence and then barely used it — and vary the acknowledgment. 'Okay, perfect' lands eleven times; by the end it reads as a metronome rather than warmth, and it is the only thing keeping this call at a 4 instead of a 5 on presence.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and reassuring, with real responsiveness to worry — the IKEA-bed question drew 'oh, no. Oh, not at all, not at all. Our movers are trained to disassemble those and we have the complete tools as well, so you don't have to worry' — and she explicitly made room for questions twice ('Yeah, go ahead' and 'Okay, anything else?'), leaving the customer at 'Okay, sounds good. Thank you'; short of a 5 because the warmth runs on one repeated phrase, the name was used twice, and the customer's one joke about her own furniture went unacknowledged.
